newsitem.title: GERMANY: Prime suspect held in German disco bombing probe.
newsitem.headline: Prime suspect held in German disco bombing probe.

text.p: German prosecutors said on Friday they had arrested a woman they believe planted a bomb in a West Berlin nightclub ten years ago which killed three people and wounded 200, including many U.S. servicemen.
Prosecutors said they had arrested the 37-year old German woman, identified only as Verena C., and her Palestinian ex-husband, Ali C., in Berlin on Thursday.
They said they believed she planted the bomb at the request of Ali C. and another suspect, Yasser Shraydi, who was extradited to Germany from Lebanon in May this year.

The United States blamed Libya for the attack on the "La Belle" disco and responded by bombing the Arab state, killing at least 15 people, including an adopted 15-month-old daughter of leader Muammar Gaddafi and wounding more than 100.
"We believe this was an act of state sponsored-terrorism," Berlin prosecutor Dieter Neumann told Reuters. "The crime was orchestrated from the Libyan embassy in East Berlin."

Neumann and his team have also issued arrest warrants for three former members of the Libyan embassy in East Berlin -- identified only by the surnames Elamin, Keshlaf and Al Abani -- and a Libyan secret service member named Rashed.
The prosecutors believe those suspects provided the explosives and helped organise the bombing but are now back in their homeland.
Two U.S. soldiers and a Turkish woman were killed in the April 1986 attack on the club in Berlin's Schoeneberg district and scores of off-duty U.S. military personnel were injured.
"This crime was planned in Libya," Neumann said. He declined to explain what had led prosecutors to the suspected bombers ten years after the attack took place.
Prosecutors' investigations appeared to have suffered a setback earlier this year when one of the key witnesses died in a car crash in Portugal.
Rainer Wiegand, a former official of the East German Stasi intelligence service, and his wife died on June 17 when their rented car was involved in a head-on collision in the south of the country.
Press reports said Wiegand had provided investigators with Stasi information on Arab guerrillas after German unification in 1990. Prosecutors have declined to comment on the reports.
